questions.text: What is a lottery in expected-utility theory?

options.a: A random process with equal probabilities for every outcome.
options.b: A choice that always causes financial loss.
options.c: A gamble that necessarily offers positive expected profit.
options.d: A set of possible outcomes associated with probabilities.

questions.text: Which property must the probabilities of a complete lottery satisfy?

options.a: Each probability must equal the corresponding monetary payoff.
options.b: Their sum can exceed one if outcomes overlap.
options.c: Each lies between zero and one and their sum equals one.
options.d: Every probability must be strictly positive.

questions.text: The expected monetary value of a lottery is what?

options.a: Its highest possible payoff.
options.b: The payoff of its median outcome regardless of probability.
options.c: The probability-weighted average of its possible payoffs.
options.d: The most likely payoff.

questions.text: A fair gamble with payoffs expressed as gains or losses relative to the status quo has which expected gain?

options.a: Equal to its payoff variance.
options.b: Zero.
options.c: Strictly negative.
options.d: Strictly positive.

questions.text: Which expression describes the variance of lottery payoffs?

options.a: The square root of expected payoff.
options.b: The difference between largest and smallest payoffs only.
options.c: The probability-weighted sum of squared deviations from the expected payoff.
options.d: The sum of unweighted payoffs.

questions.text: How is the standard deviation of lottery payoffs related to their variance?

options.a: It is the positive square root of variance.
options.b: It always equals expected utility.
options.c: It is variance squared.
options.d: It is the expected payoff divided by variance.

questions.text: Which comparison better isolates risk rather than average payoff?

options.a: Two lotteries with different expected payoffs and identical dispersion.
options.b: Two lotteries with equal expected payoffs but different dispersion.
options.c: Two outcomes that are both certain.
options.d: Two fixed payments with identical amounts and dates.

questions.text: Why can a risk-averse person reject a lottery with a positive expected monetary gain?

options.a: Risk aversion implies the expected monetary payoff is negative.
options.b: Risk aversion prohibits any consumption in bad states.
options.c: Expected utility, not merely expected money, drives the decision.
options.d: Expected utility cannot be defined over wealth.

questions.text: What is a state of nature?

options.a: A possible realization of an uncertain event.
options.b: A fixed price of an asset.
options.c: An unchangeable preference parameter.
options.d: A jurisdiction where insurance is sold.

questions.text: What is a contingent consumption plan?

options.a: A budget line without uncertainty.
options.b: Consumption determined only after probabilities become equal.
options.c: Consumption specified separately for each possible state of nature.
options.d: A plan to consume equal amounts of every good in every year.

questions.text: In the insurance model, purchasing additional coverage K with premium rate gamma generally does what?

options.a: Lowers wealth in the loss state but raises it in the no-loss state.
options.b: Raises wealth equally in both states with no cost.
options.c: Eliminates the probability of loss.
options.d: Raises wealth in the loss state net of premium and lowers wealth in the no-loss state.

questions.text: If a person has wealth W, loss L, insurance coverage K and premium gamma K, wealth in the loss state is what?

options.a: W - L - K + gamma K.
options.b: W - L + K - gamma K.
options.c: W + K without premiums.
options.d: W + L - K.

questions.text: Under the same contract, wealth in the no-loss state is what?

options.a: W - L + K.
options.b: W - gamma K.
options.c: W - L - gamma K.
options.d: W + K + gamma K.

questions.text: With insurance premium gamma per unit of coverage, what is the slope of the insurance opportunity line when good-state wealth is vertical and bad-state wealth is horizontal?

options.a: -(1-gamma)/gamma.
options.b: -gamma/(1-gamma).
options.c: -1/gamma for all gamma.
options.d: -gamma.

questions.text: Why can insurance improve welfare without changing the probability of an accident?

options.a: It converts a risky technology into a sure technology.
options.b: It necessarily increases the expected monetary payoff.
options.c: It redistributes resources from a good state to a bad state.
options.d: It raises the objective probability of all good states.

questions.text: A two-state von Neumann-Morgenstern expected utility function has which form?

options.a: v(pi1 c1 + pi2 c2) for all preferences.
options.b: v(c1) + v(c2) without probabilities.
options.c: pi1 c1 times pi2 c2 for all preferences.
options.d: pi1 v(c1) + pi2 v(c2).

questions.text: Why is expected utility additive across mutually exclusive states?

options.a: Every consumer must be risk neutral.
options.b: Probabilities can be ignored.
options.c: Consumers always consume both states simultaneously.
options.d: The independence assumption permits state outcomes to enter separately with probability weights.

questions.text: Which transformation preserves the expected-utility representation of a utility index?

options.a: A positive affine transformation, a v + b with a greater than zero.
options.b: Every strictly increasing nonlinear transformation of the von Neumann-Morgenstern index.
options.c: Taking any decreasing transformation.
options.d: Multiplying the index by a negative constant.

questions.text: Why is a strictly increasing nonlinear transformation of a von Neumann-Morgenstern index generally problematic?

options.a: It can change preferences over lotteries even if it preserves the ranking of certain outcomes.
options.b: It always reverses preferences over certain outcomes.
options.c: It forces all lotteries to have zero variance.
options.d: It makes probabilities sum to more than one.

questions.text: What is the relevant objective in expected-utility maximization?

options.a: The utility of the maximum payoff only.
options.b: The probability of the worst state alone.
options.c: The highest monetary payoff regardless of likelihood.
options.d: The probability-weighted utility of state-contingent outcomes.

questions.text: For a strictly risk-averse person, which utility curvature characterizes utility of wealth?

options.a: Strict concavity.
options.b: A step function that is necessarily increasing in risk.
options.c: Strict convexity.
options.d: Constant marginal utility with no curvature.

questions.text: For a risk-loving person, which curvature characterizes utility of wealth in the standard model?

options.a: Convexity.
options.b: Verticality of all indifference curves.
options.c: Strict concavity.
options.d: Linearity only.

questions.text: For a risk-neutral person, utility of wealth may be represented by which functional form?

options.a: A constant function that values no outcomes.
options.b: A strictly concave function only.
options.c: A strictly convex function only.
options.d: A linear function of wealth.

questions.text: Which inequality expresses risk aversion for a nondegenerate wealth lottery?

options.a: u(E[W]) is at least E[u(W)].
options.b: E[u(W)] always exceeds u(E[W]).
options.c: u(E[W]) equals the maximum utility in every state.
options.d: u(E[W]) is necessarily zero.

questions.text: For a strictly risk-averse individual considering a nondegenerate fair gamble in wealth, what is preferred?

options.a: Taking the gamble regardless of its size.
options.b: Keeping certain wealth rather than accepting the fair gamble.
options.c: The worst outcome of the gamble.
options.d: Being indifferent in all cases.

questions.text: What does Jensen's inequality imply for concave Bernoulli utility?

options.a: Expected utility exceeds utility at expected wealth.
options.b: Expected wealth must be negative.
options.c: Utility at expected wealth is at least expected utility of wealth.
options.d: Variance must equal zero.

questions.text: A risk-neutral decision maker compares lotteries mainly by what?

options.a: Payoff variance only.
options.b: Expected monetary payoff.
options.c: The lowest possible payoff only.
options.d: Skewness regardless of expected payoff.

questions.text: What effect does increasing dispersion of payoffs at unchanged mean have on a risk-averse person's expected utility, under a mean-preserving spread?

options.a: It makes the person's expected wealth rise.
options.b: It necessarily raises expected utility.
options.c: It leaves expected utility unchanged for every strictly concave utility.
options.d: It weakly lowers expected utility.

questions.text: What is a certainty equivalent of a risky lottery?

options.a: A payment that makes the lottery riskless for society.
options.b: The minimum possible lottery payoff by definition.
options.c: The sure wealth amount delivering the same utility as the lottery's expected utility.
options.d: The largest lottery payoff.

questions.text: For a risk-averse consumer, how does the certainty equivalent typically compare with the lottery's expected payoff?

options.a: It is below the expected payoff for a nondegenerate lottery under strict concavity.
options.b: It always equals the maximum outcome.
options.c: It is above expected payoff.
options.d: It always equals expected payoff regardless of risk.

questions.text: How is a lottery's risk premium usually defined?

options.a: Variance multiplied by probability.
options.b: Expected payoff minus certainty equivalent.
options.c: Minimum payoff minus mean payoff.
options.d: Certainty equivalent minus maximum payoff.

questions.text: For a strictly risk-averse decision maker facing a risky lottery, the risk premium is generally what?

options.a: Identical to the lottery's standard deviation.
options.b: Always zero.
options.c: Positive.
options.d: Negative.

questions.text: For a risk-neutral person, the risk premium for a fair lottery is what?

options.a: Always positive.
options.b: Always negative.
options.c: Equal to the expected loss.
options.d: Zero.

questions.text: For a risk-loving person, the risk premium defined as expected wealth minus certainty equivalent is typically what?

options.a: Zero regardless of uncertainty.
options.b: Negative.
options.c: Positive.
options.d: Equal to the loss probability.

questions.text: A consumer has utility u(W) = sqrt(W). What happens to marginal utility as wealth increases?

options.a: It decreases, consistent with risk aversion.
options.b: It remains constant, consistent with neutrality.
options.c: It increases, consistent with risk loving.
options.d: It becomes negative for any positive wealth.

questions.text: An actuarially fair insurance premium per euro of coverage equals what?

options.a: The consumer's wealth level.
options.b: The possible monetary loss itself.
options.c: One minus the probability of loss.
options.d: The probability of the insured loss.

questions.text: For a strictly risk-averse individual with fair insurance and a fixed possible loss, what is the standard optimum?

options.a: Coverage designed to maximize wealth variance.
options.b: Full insurance, equalizing wealth across states.
options.c: Coverage strictly greater than any possible loss by necessity.
options.d: No insurance regardless of preferences.

questions.text: Why does equalizing consumption across states characterize full insurance?

options.a: It changes loss probability to zero.
options.b: It removes consumption risk while preserving expected resources under fair pricing.
options.c: It maximizes variance.
options.d: It eliminates premiums altogether.

questions.text: If the insurance premium exceeds the actuarially fair rate, what does this mean for the insurer's expected profit per unit?

options.a: It is positive before expenses, given the model's assumptions.
options.b: It must equal the consumer's risk premium.
options.c: It is negative by definition.
options.d: It is exactly zero by definition.

questions.text: When insurance is unfairly priced, which statement is most accurate?

options.a: No consumer can ever buy insurance.
options.b: Full insurance must still maximize expected utility regardless of premium.
options.c: A risk-averse consumer may rationally choose partial insurance rather than full insurance.
options.d: Every risk-averse consumer must buy full insurance.

questions.text: Why can a small positive expected monetary return fail to compensate a person for taking risk?

options.a: All consumers have constant marginal utility.
options.b: A positive return rules out negative outcomes.
options.c: The utility cost of variability may exceed the expected monetary gain.
options.d: The lottery must be actuarially fair.

questions.text: What is the optimality condition for an interior purchase of contingent consumption via insurance?

options.a: The marginal rate of substitution across states equals the insurance trade-off rate.
options.b: The insurance premium must be zero.
options.c: The marginal utility in the good state must be zero.
options.d: The two states must have equal probabilities.

questions.text: Why does the wealth distribution become certain when full insurance is actuarially fair in the simple two-state model?

options.a: Wealth after premiums equals W minus the expected loss in both states.
options.b: The loss probability becomes one.
options.c: The insurance contract removes the physical loss.
options.d: The household pays a premium only if the accident occurs.

questions.text: If a consumer's utility is concave, what does the consumer generally prefer between a certain €100 and a risky lottery with mean €100?

options.a: Indifference in every case.
options.b: The lottery in every case.
options.c: The lottery only because its variance is positive.
options.d: The certain €100, with strict preference under strict concavity and nonzero risk.

questions.text: What attitude toward risk is represented by the displayed curvature of utility of wealth?

options.a: Risk loving, because utility is convex in wealth.
options.b: Risk neutrality, because utility is linear.
options.c: An inability to compare lotteries.
options.d: Risk aversion, because utility is concave in wealth.
